answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate the strongest-precedent option: memory_b1 (rollback) is the closest match to a post-release latency/error climb, but compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so it is unavailable regardless of its track record. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fail fast by design — during settlement peak with heavy writes that directly conflicts with the 'without losing customer writes' constraint, so it is the wrong instrument here. Regional failover (memory_b2) recovered a latency degradation quickly, but that record concerns latency/error rates, not write durability; shifting a write-heavy path at daily peak risks in-flight and replication-lagged writes. Add capacity (memory_b3) is attractive but that memory describes headroom provisioned BEFORE a known peak, not capacity added mid-incident; provisioning latency likely exceeds the useful window and it does not address a contention cause. Route reads to replicas (memory_b5) is the only option whose recorded mechanism matches this symptom precisely — offloading read/reporting load from the primary and recovering transactional WRITE latency same day — and it is non-destructive and reversible with no write-loss surface. That is why I spend my one verification on memory_b5: it is the load-bearing memory, and I need the original record to confirm (a) the recovery was actually attributable to the read offload rather than a coincident traffic drop, and (b) the day-55 primary was under read contention comparable to today's, rather than a different bottleneck (lock contention, IO saturation, or a regression introduced by the new build itself). Important uncertainty I am not resolving: the latency climb began roughly when the release shipped, which makes a build-induced write regression a live competing hypothesis that read offload would only mask, not fix. Also note the inherited memory set is uniformly success stories — six wins, zero recorded failures — which is a survivorship pattern; I am treating these as weaker evidence than their confident tone suggests. Downstream value risk: shifting reads to replicas introduces stale-read exposure, and if any settlement, balance, or reconciliation logic reads through those paths, correctness errors could propagate silently into financial records — worse than latency. I therefore scope this as a small guarded test: route only dashboard/reporting read traffic, explicitly exclude any read path feeding settlement or authorization decisions, watch primary write p99 for 10-15 minutes, and expand only if the causal link holds. If write latency does not respond, that is strong evidence for the release-regression hypothesis and the next window should target the build (forward fix, not revert) rather than more infrastructure moves.
